content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes an efficient Transformer that squeezes visual tokens via semantic information as for key/value tokens. This clustering-guided way to conduct self-attention benefits the reduction of computational complexity. Besides, varying the token reduction ratio introduces multi-scale mechanism that fits the nature of dense prediction tasks. Finally, the paper instantiates three variants of their model ClusTR, namely ClusTR-T, ClusTR-S, ClusTR-B. The versatile Transformer backbone outperforms the current state-of-the-art on a series of vision tasks including ImageNet classification, ADE20k segmentation, COCO detection, and COCOWholeBody pose estimation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: 
+ The paper has a clear motivation that makes self-attention operation efficient and sparse. Accordingly, the authors propose a new transformer architecture. 
+ This work displays comprehensive and favorable results on several vision tasks, including image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation. 
+ The ablation studies on grid-based and proposed clustering demonstrate the effectiveness in terms of both performance and computational cost.
+ This paper is easy to follow, and the figure is vivid and informative.

Weakness:
- Grouping idea is not novel in terms of Transformers, where it is not necessary to compute the whole attention maps. Many works [1][2][3] leverage this methodology to empower the Transformer, thus limiting the technical contribution.
- The way of clustering is not straightforward. As we know, attention prefers to interact with which tokens are similar to itself.  Therefore, previous works like [1][4] which conduct ''local'' self-attention inside the cluster sound reasonable to me. However, the proposed method tries to aggregate the tokens across the clusters without any intra-cluster interaction.  
- The performance is not comparable with DGT [1], which also takes the grouping as their main contribution. For instance, DGT-T reaches 83.8% Top1 ImageNet accuracy with only 24M parameters and 4.3G flops. It may result from the wrong way to cluster the tokens.

[1] Dynamic Group Transformer: A General Vision Transformer Backbone with Dynamic Group Attention. IJCAI 2022.

[2] GroupViT: Semantic Segmentation Emerges from Text Supervision. CVPR 2022.

[3] Reformer: The Efficient Transformer. ICLR 2020.

[4] Vision Transformer with Deformable Attention. CVPR 2022.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is easy to follow and the method is well demonstrated. From my perspective, the methodology somewhat lacks originality and quality. It is not original that the self-attention operation works in the partition fashion and it is not required to compute the dense attention maps.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper improves self-attention via clustering the tokens so that reducing the computation cost. The methodology of grouping is somewhat not novel. The specific formulation is not reasonable to me as stated in the weakness part. Thus, my initial rating would be rejection.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper provides a novel vision Transformer architecture, called ClusTR, that focuses on resolving the computational complexity issue mainly caused within the self-attention modules. In order to address the aforementioned issue, the authors introduced a content-based sparse attention model (as opposed to dense self-attention). In specific, the key and value tokens within the attention module is being clustered and aggregated to lessen the number of overall tokens. The proposed method outperformed the baseline SOTA methods in terms of accuracy while maintaining lower computational cost + fewer parameters.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- Reasonable attempt to reconstruct the self-attention mechanism to reduce the computational complexity 
- The idea about choosing to go with clustering to cut down computation for self-attention was simple and clever.

Weaknesses:
- This paper requires more work on providing more cut-to-the-chase explanation
- Most (if not all) of the experiments are focused on measuring the performances on different dataset. The proposed claim would be more convincing if the paper included experiments that focuses on ablations on the proposed modules. I would also like to see XX experiments. - What was the motivation behind using the kNN-based approach among other available clustering methods?
- I would like to see more discussions on what is being leveraged through the clustering process. While the quantitative results do show that the approach does better than the baselines in multiple tasks, the authors have failed to deliver why/how having representative clusters assist in acquiring better accuracy. 
- It would be more effective if the paper included a discussion on the constraints of limited self-attention range. The authors mentioned in Section 2 that the proposed method encourages exploration of global attention patterns. - The performance gains are relatively incremental. - How does the new attention provided by the ClusAtt affect the overall attention when compared to a vanilla version.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- When does the clustering actually happen? Is it part of the overall end-to-end architecture?  Clarity on this could be helpful.

- In terms of reproducibility, the papers provides reasonable amount of details to replicate the results. - In terms of novelty, I have found an ICML paper called, “Fast Transformers with Clustered Attention” (https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.04825) which also talk about leveraging cluster centroids within the attention module. This paper has not been included nor discussed in the submitted manuscript.
content.summary_of_the_review: Based on the weaknesses (listed above), I would like to mention that the paper needs additional components before it can be accepted at this venue.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper presents an efficient vision transformer **ClusTR** which uses clustering to aggregate similar key and value tokens. The reduced number of key/value tokens used for attention computation improves the efficiency of vision transformers. The paper further extends this to multi-scale clustering where a different number of reduction factors help aggregate features at different scales. This is shown to improve the performance for dense prediction tasks such as segmentation. 

The paper argues that in contrast to grid-based token aggregation explored in [1], clustering key/value tokens preserves the diversity of the tokens and is less affected by background/large objects. This could be particularly beneficial for detecting/segmenting small objects. Experiments are conducted on a wide variety of vision tasks including classification, segmentation, detection, and pose estimation.

[1] Pyramid vision transformer: A versatile backbone for dense prediction without convolutions. ICCV 2021
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**:
  - The proposed method is easy and the performance on the vision tasks shows that for a similar number of parameters, the combination of multi-scaling and clustering-based aggregation outperforms recent Transformer and Convolutional baselines to achieve state-of-the-art performance on diverse vision tasks.
  - The method is evaluated on a diverse set of tasks. I also appreciate the visualization of clustering presented in the Appendix.

**Questions and Weakness**:
  - The paper often lacks clarity. Some of the examples are provided below:
    - It is not clear if the clustering is applied to (a) original sequence $X$, (b) independently to the keys $K$ and values $V$, or (c) just one of the key/value and the cluster indices are reused. From the paper, it looks to be (b) (kindly correct me if I misunderstood). In the case of (b), it is not clear to me how the correspondence between clustered keys and values is maintained. In regular attention, there is an implicit one-to-one correspondence between the key and value at the same index.
    - Choice of clustering: kNN-based density peaks clustering is not well motivated.  No theoretical or experimental argument is presented against something like euclidean distance-based k-means clustering.  Also, the complexity of the clustering step is not presented. From equations, it seems that distances for all pairs of points need to be calculated which would lead to the same computation cost as regular attention. Did I miss something?  Is clustering done separately for all layers in a stage?
    - FLOPs calculation: It is not clear if the FLOPs calculation includes the clustering step. It would be good to show this calculation at least in the Appendix.
  - FLOPs does not completely reflect efficiency:
    - The paper presents FLOPs as a metric to measure compute efficiency, but FLOPs being a theoretical metric for efficiency do not capture the actual running times which may differ substantially on GPU and CPU. It would be advised to also include the inference or training time/latency and memory results in the experiments.
  - Missing references and comparisons:
    - The paper currently misses to refer/compare against some very close works that use clustering to reduce the cost of attention computation. Some of these are listed below. The two works which are close to the proposed method include [2] which proposes to cluster queries to reduce the attention computation. In [3], adaptive clustering is explored for DETR with ResNet backbone for the object detection task.

References:

[1] Pyramid vision transformer: A versatile backbone for dense prediction without convolutions. ICCV 2021

[2] Fast Transformers with Clustered Attention. NeurIPS 2020

[3] End-to-End Object Detection with Adaptive Clustering Transformer. BMVC 2021

[4] SMYRF - Efficient Attention using Asymmetric Clustering. NeurIPS 2020

[5] Sparse Attention with Learning-to-Hash. ICLR 2021
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is generally easy to follow, however, it currently lacks some details (see above). It should be able to reproduce this work once these details are added/clarified. The proposal of multi-scale clusters is novel, however, clustering itself has been explored in several works to improve the efficiency of Transformers.
content.summary_of_the_review: This work introduces a simple technique that uses clustering to aggregate semantically similar keys and values for attention computation with a reduced number of tokens. I have recommended rejection due to the following reasons.  First, the paper lacks some novelty. While multi-scale clustering is novel, efficient attention using clustering has been explored before. Second, the paper has not referred to or compared against the closely related clustering-based attentions. Finally, the paper currently lacks details on FLOPs calculation, inference time, and memory.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
